title: Bromcom - 355,051 breached accounts
summary: In September 2026, UK education software provider Bromcom suffered a data breach involving a legacy single sign-on (SSO) registration system. The incident exposed 355k unique email addresses belonging to staff and pupils at UK schools, alongside SSO registration reference numbers. Bromcom confirmed that no passwords or authentication tokens were exposed, and that the incident did not enable access to Microsoft or Google accounts or its school management system.

title: Too Lost - 724,323 breached accounts
summary: In November 2026, an unauthorised party claimed to have obtained data from the music distributor for independent artists, Too Lost. The data contained 724k unique email addresses belonging to artists, their collaborators and fans. Some records also contained bcrypt password hashes, while a small subset included partial credit card data (last 4 digits and card type), identity verification information (in some cases, passport, driver's licence or national ID numbers), and payouts made to artists. Too Lost advised that its investigation remains ongoing, external forensic specialists have been engaged, and measures have been taken to secure affected systems and credentials. The company is also working with advisors to coordinate communications and support for affected individuals.

title: Take me to the fatberg! The £437m new Museum of London is an astonishing sight
summary:
After a 10-year transformation, the glorious cathedral-like Smithfields market is now telling the capital’s story. Our architecture critic enters a world of jewels, axes, DJs and dog races – with unposh coffee from Syd’s century-old stall

‘All the grit and the glitters,” trumpets a big illuminated sign on the roof of the old Smithfield general market, beaming out as if advertising a raunchy burlesque show. It is the jazzy tagline of the new-look London Museum, which has gone from being marooned on a roundabout in an armpit of the City to taking over this prime Victorian market complex, following an arduous decade-long transformation.

The slogan is fitting for a museum that displays everything from priceless Tudor jewels to a lump of congealed fat and rags dredged from a Whitechapel sewer. Just as the colossal fatberg was scraped from the murky depths, so has the former market hall (and its extensive warren of basement vaults) been meticulously scoured and scrubbed up. London’s centre of butchery for 800 years, which Charles Dickens found “all asmear with filth and fat and blood and foam”, has been lavished with a £437m glow-up, reborn to tell the story of the capital in all its gritty, glittery glory. And the finished result is an astonishing sight.

The scenes in a Liverpool Marks & Spencer, after the release of the chain’s chocolate and cornflake cookie earlier this month, looked like brink-of-Covid panic buying crossed with a zombie apocalypse. It probably didn’t help that the baked goods hit the shelves at around the time the government started asking Britons to plan for an unnamed near-term disaster. How would we cope with a national emergency when we coped this badly with the crisis of not enough biscuits?

You could explain the M&S cookie fever with reference to the company’s product development icon, Kathryn Turner, who has half a million followers between Instagram and TikTok, or the powerful urge to belong, in gen Z particularly. But it surely has something to do with the biscuit itself. As Rosie Sykes, the author of The Friday Biscuit, says: “Biscuits are very much part of the national fabric.” But lately they’ve had this “slightly weird glow-up”, gone “a bit max”, Sykes says. Whatever the flavour, there is always chocolate in them, and always more of it than you’d credit. Even the packaging on the M&S cookies – clear, crinkly – has the main-event feel of a bouquet or a hamper. title: Sweden’s datacentre politics are more complicated than they appear | Letter
summary:
There are distinct tensions over who controls, benefits from and gains access to natural and public resources, write James White and Nora Söderberg

Steve Rose’s account of Sweden’s datacentre sector (‘Datacentres are deeply unpopular. Has Sweden made one we can all love?’, 12 November) is a welcome reminder that digital infrastructure can be developed in more environmentally responsible ways. However, his suggestion that datacentres have become politically contentious elsewhere, “but here in Sweden, not so much”, is a misrepresentation.

Consider the proposed Google datacentre development at Torsboda, near Sundsvall, which requires an enormous allocation of electricity and industrial land. The StoppaGoogle campaign, initiated by the regional political party Norrlandspartiet, has been vocal in challenging what this development will mean for electricity prices, employment and regional development.

Controversy over datacentres in Sweden’s north reflect wider debate about resource extraction for the green and technological transitions, and the worry that Sweden is becoming an “electricity colony” of big tech, providing cheap, green energy while the economic benefits are realised elsewhere.

At the same time, Sweden-based researchers, such as Julia Velkova, and Jutta Haider and Malte Rödl, have argued that the sustainability of digital infrastructure cannot be reduced to carbon emissions and technological efficiency. Datacentres place high demands on electricity grids, necessitating government investment and compromising access for other industries, communities and public services. While these direct impacts of datacentres are important, so too are the downstream consequences that they overshadow, including how digital services promote climate disinformation and unsustainable mass consumption.

Sweden’s renewable energy infrastructure does not make datacentre development environmentally or politically unproblematic, but contributes to distinct tensions over who controls, benefits from and gains access to natural and public resources.

Rather than presenting Sweden as an exception to the growing politicisation of datacentres, we should recognise how these conflicts emerge differently in different places, shaped by their histories, infrastructures and political economies.
James White and Nora Söderberg

Nine months later, Kalshi’s grip on American fans appears murderously tight: notional monthly trading volume on the platform, the majority of which is taken up by wagers on sports, increased to nearly $100bn in October from $40bn in August, as the company gears up for yet another funding round at a rumored valuation of $65bn ahead of a potential IPO. However righteous the disgust from fans on social media at the deepening incursion of these odious platforms into professional sport may be, their popularity seems only to grow.

More perplexing is the widening circle of athletes like Giannis who’ve thrown off whatever shame might once have come from association with these businesses and given them their full-throated support. The line between role model and shill in professional sports is now essentially non-existent. Pete Sampras, a man so private in retirement it can often seem like his entire tennis career was a collective hallucination, released an ad for Kalshi during this year’s US Open after two decades largely out of the public eye. LeBron James will make more from his recently announced partnership with Polymarket – $15m a year – than he will from playing for the Philadelphia 76ers. At its centre, receiving its world premiere, was The Travelling Violin by the jazz bassist and composer Misha Mullov-Abbado. In four movements, it’s an almost-concerto on an intimate scale. The solo violin, deftly played here by Tamsin Waley-Cohen, has the narrating role, but the writing for the nine supporting string instruments is so intricately woven that it feels like an ensemble piece. It almost seemed strange for Waley-Cohen to give a solo encore at the end, mesmerising though her playing of Nicola Matteis Jr’s A minor Fantasia was.

Mullov-Abbado’s piece has a role for jazz bass, which he played himself, and for percussion, from soft-edged shimmering to driving, grooving drums, played by Fred Thomas; the jazz sensibility of both of these leaches into the rest. Led by the violinist Julian Azkoul, the ensemble was tight, churning over the tricksy rhythmic figures of the faster movements and radiating warmth in the third, which sounded like Cole Porter reflected in a slightly warped mirror. title: Will the Jilly Cooper plagiarism allegations taint our love of Rivals? I doubt it | Nadia Khomami

“Immature poets imitate; mature poets steal,” the poet TS Eliot wrote a century ago. No work of art, he argued, exists in a vacuum. Great writers draw on what came before them, transforming their influences into something entirely their own.

Eliot’s words came to mind when I read the revelations about the queen of the country house bonkbuster Jilly Cooper, who has been accused of “extensive and deliberate” plagiarism in her 1978 book Prudence. At least 35 passages appear to have been lifted from The Serial, a satirical novel by American writer Cyra McFadden, alongside remarkable similarities to sections of Josephine Tey’s 1948 novel The Franchise Affair. McFadden’s daughter is threatening legal action, describing the treatment of her mother’s work as “unconscionable”.

In GTA VI, Rockstar has created the most extraordinarily, indulgently detailed virtual world that we have yet seen. Reviewing it feels a bit like trying to review, say, Paris: it contains so many potential experiences that it’s hard to know where to start. If you had been spying on me playing this game over the past few weeks you may well have caught me robbing banks, shooting up a weed farm or tearing along the highway at sunset blaring Bad Bunny on the in-game radio, but you might equally have caught me doing squats at the gym, shopping, assembling a coffee table or walking along the beach eating ice-cream. There is such a multiplicity of things on offer here that it is difficult to nail down what this game definitively is. Is it an interactive crime movie? A city simulator? A driving game? A sort of absurdly expansive version of The Sims in which the people you’re dressing up and looking after just happen to be professional criminals? It will be different for everyone – that is the beauty of it.

For me, though, this game is about Jason and Lucia, the fugitive couple through whom you experience all that Leonida has to offer. This ecstatic condition is named after the French novelist who in 1817 fell ill in Florence, after gorging on the beauty of the Renaissance city’s treasures until “I had palpitations of the heart … I walked with the fear of falling”. Goldin, too, has suffered a bout of this aesthetic delirium, not in Italy but Paris – “the first time I was alone in the Louvre”, she explains on screen.

title: Crunch time: Niki Segnit’s five rules for winter salads
summary:

Approach a winter salad as you would your winter wardrobe – with clever layering. With the greatest respect to Coco Chanel, and her famous rule about taking one item off when you think you’re done, in this instance I favour assembling a salad and then adding an ingredient. Unlike in baking, where departing from a recipe can have its risks, improvisation rewards the salad maker. Still, if you’re planning a winter salad, especially if it’s a main meal, you might want to use a checklist to avoid some common pitfalls.

The most egregious of these is cosy dullness. It’s all too easy to throw together some fresh winter produce and end up with a dish that’s more like a cold risotto or yesterday’s traybake. This often comes down to the combination of roasted root vegetables and “interesting” grains. What makes a salad a salad is its invigorating qualities, but root veg and cereals are sweet, with earthy, nutty flavours and soft textures; the pairing might be a modern classic but it’s about as invigorating as a warm bath. Not that you should avoid the combination; you just want to balance it with ingredients that offset its soporific qualities. It’s a good stress test for our guidelines, in fact: if you can turn a root-and-grain combination into a bright and balanced salad, you’re on to a winner.

‘Tequila?” says a woman brightly, proffering a pink plastic shot glass. It’s barely 10.30 on a Saturday morning, and my perimenopause wellness journey is not going entirely as expected. We are standing in a neon-lit London conference centre amid the hubbub of Pause Live, billed as the UK’s biggest annual women’s health and menopause event and essentially a consumer fair for those in midlife. All around me, women are sampling free squirts of menthol lotion (supposed to cool hot flushes) and paper thimblefuls of slightly grainy, sweet latte made with powdered Peruvian maca root instead of coffee.

The tequila, it turns out, is a gift from the sponsors, with no miracle ingredients beyond alcohol. But stalls offer everything from neck creams to pelvic-floor trainers, mindfulness journals and hairpieces for disguising thinning locks, plus herbal supplements in every conceivable edible form: chocolate truffles, ginger shots, mushroom coffee. (Fungi are big news in the menopause wellness world, often touted as an answer to brain fog. Though at best the scientific jury is still out, Ocado searches for lion’s mane mushrooms more than quadrupled after an episode of Clarkson’s Farm in which Jeremy Clarkson’s partner, Lisa Hogan, persuaded him to grow them to make supplements, claiming that “everyone who’s anyone” is on them.)

And if the city never quite freezes over in the coldest months – except for the blizzard of the century that came with Storm Filomena in 2021 – it is also said that the subtle, evil wind coming in from the mountains could kill a person without snuffing a candle.

Personally, I prefer it here at this time of year, though if you’re looking to escape the crowds you might be disappointed. Madrid has only got busier in the 11 years I’ve lived here, and Christmas feels more crowded than midsummer on the central streets around Puerta del Sol. All the main public squares get their own giant Christmas trees, while Plaza de España and Plaza Colón install ice rinks too, and a festive market fills the cobbled core of Plaza Mayor with painted wooden huts. Mentally replaying that game in my head, flashing back to the many scenes involving such things as smoking meth, over-the-top gratuitous violence and grubby sex in one character’s trailer, I said “no way”. Later I gently mentioned to the kid’s mother that GTA V was an 18-rated game and really wasn’t suitable for kids. “Oh, but he’s really good at these games,” she told me. She was genuinely shocked to learn that an 18-rating on a video game was a flag for adult content, rather than an indication of its difficulty.

Grand Theft Auto VI is released this week. It is an incredible creative and technical feat, conjuring a realistic-looking and exhaustively detailed virtual Florida filled with every kind of filth and criminality you could imagine. It is brilliant, entertainingly observed and even sometimes unexpectedly touching, largely thanks to a central love story between the player couple, Jason and Lucia. It is lewd, violent and frequently hilarious. It is also absolutely full of stuff that I really would not want my 10 and seven-year-old boys to see or hear.
